action_criteria.expected_evidence: Complete AV block with AV dissociation and a wide ventricular escape at 35 bpm (RBBB morphology, left axis deviation)
action_criteria.label: Obtain a 12-lead ECG on arrival
action_criteria.rationale: The ECG is the first test in syncope; third-degree AV block on it is diagnostic of arrhythmic syncope and calls for immediate monitoring and pacing (ESC 2018).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Potassium 4.4 mEq/L normal and creatinine 1.3 mg/dL (CKD 3a): no electrolyte cause of the block; troponin I not elevated
action_criteria.label: Electrolytes and renal function (BMP)
action_criteria.rationale: Hyperkalaemia is a reversible cause of AV block to exclude before permanent pacing, and renal function guides apixaban and metformin around the implant (ESC 2018 targeted laboratory testing; ESC 2021 pacing).

action_criteria.rationale: Known coronary disease: echocardiography is Class I in suspected structural heart disease, and LVEF decides between conventional pacing, CRT and an ICD (ESC 2018; ESC 2021 pacing).

action_criteria.rationale: Syncope with complete AV block is high risk: immediate in-hospital monitoring is Class I until pacing, and it documents the symptom-rhythm correlation and excludes VT (ESC 2018).

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give or continue AV-nodal blocking drugs (beta-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin) before pacing is secured
Do not discharge before a permanent pacemaker is implanted
Do not delay pacing for outpatient follow-up or a beta-blocker washout
Do not bridge apixaban with heparin for the device implantation
required_recommendations: Recognise persistent complete (third-degree) AV block with a wide ventricular escape, from conduction-system disease, as the cause of the syncope
Admit to a monitored bed with continuous ECG monitoring and transcutaneous pacing pads; temporary transvenous pacing if he becomes haemodynamically unstable or has further syncope before implantation

Implant a permanent pacemaker during this admission (ESC 2021 Class I for third-degree AV block without a reversible cause); with LVEF 45% and an expected near-complete ventricular pacing burden, choose the pacing mode with the electrophysiology team (CRT is preferred when LVEF is 40% or lower) and follow LVEF after implantation

Hold metoprolol until he is paced, without delaying pacing for a washout (the wide escape indicates infranodal block that persists); resume a beta-blocker for atrial fibrillation rate control and coronary disease once paced

Plan peri-procedural anticoagulation for apixaban without heparin bridging, and review the aspirin on top of apixaban 4 years after PCI (ESC 2024 AF: anticoagulant monotherapy beyond 12 months in chronic coronary disease)
Advise no driving until the pacemaker is implanted; Group 1 drivers may resume 1 week after implantation (ESC 2018)

avoided_actions.rationale: No fever, meningism or encephalopathy: CSF has no role; the syncope is explained by persistent complete AV block with a wide ventricular escape.
EEG is not recommended in syncope (ESC 2018 Class III); there were no seizure features and the cause is persistent complete AV block with a wide ventricular escape.
Brain MRI is not indicated in syncope without focal signs (ESC 2018 Class III); the cause is persistent complete AV block with a wide ventricular escape, and the head injury is assessed by CT.
Tilt testing does not confirm cardiac syncope; persistent complete AV block with a wide ventricular escape is documented on the ECG and monitoring.
The pacing indication is established by persistent complete AV block with a wide ventricular escape; exercise testing adds no decision.

differential.key_features: Prior anterior infarct is a substrate, but 24 h of telemetry shows only isolated PVCs, LVEF is 45%, and the symptoms coincided with slow complete heart block.
He takes metoprolol, but the wide escape with RBBB morphology and left axis deviation indicates infranodal conduction disease, which a beta-blocker neither causes nor reverses on withdrawal.
Paroxysmal AF can cause conversion pauses, but telemetry shows AV dissociation with a regular wide escape in sinus rhythm and in AF: the mechanism is AV block.

Ischaemia is a reversible cause of AV block, but there is no chest pain or ST elevation, troponin I is not elevated, and the wide escape indicates infranodal disease rather than nodal block of inferior infarction.
Collapse while seated without prodrome or trigger, with complete AV block on the ECG; not vasovagal.
The collapse occurred seated and the near-syncope on telemetry was seated at 30-32 bpm; complete AV block explains the events.

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.
results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948)

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.
results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope (Shen WK et al.)

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

Lenegre-Lev disease (idiopathic degenerative fibrosis of the conduction system) is the most common cause of acquired complete heart block in the elderly

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Gerald Whitfield is a 70-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes who was brought to the emergency department by EMS after his wife witnessed him suddenly collapse at home. The patient was seated at the kitchen table eating breakfast at approximately 8:15 AM when he suddenly slumped forward and fell to the floor without any preceding warning. His wife, who was standing nearby, reports that there was no cry out, no tonic posturing, and no rhythmic jerking of the extremities. She states he appeared pale and 'looked gray' during the event. He was unresponsive for approximately 20-30 seconds before regaining consciousness. Upon awakening, he was immediately alert and oriented, asking what had happened. There was no period of confusion, no tongue biting, and no urinary incontinence. He sustained a small forehead laceration from striking the kitchen floor. The patient reports that over the past three weeks he has experienced two prior episodes of 'nearly blacking out' characterized by sudden lightheadedness and a sensation that the room was going dark, each lasting only a few seconds. He did not lose consciousness during those episodes but had to sit down. He has also noticed increasing fatigue and mild exertional dyspnea when walking to the mailbox over the past two months. He denies chest pain, palpitations preceding the event, or recent illness. He reports a past episode of palpitations several months ago but was told his atrial fibrillation was 'controlled.' His wife confirms that he has never had a seizure before and that this episode looked distinctly different from seizures she witnessed her late sister experience.

neurological_exam.additional: No tongue laceration or oral trauma. No signs of urinary incontinence. No bruising to suggest prolonged convulsive activity. Small laceration on right forehead from fall, hemostasis achieved.

CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with activation. CN VIII: Hearing grossly intact to finger rub bilaterally. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically, gag reflex intact. CN XI: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue midline, no fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady, normal base. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative. No ataxia.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Speech is fluent with normal rate and prosody. No dysarthria. Attention intact, able to spell WORLD backwards. Recall 3/3 objects at 5 minutes. No confusion or post-ictal features at time of examination.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal in all extremities, no rigidity or spasticity. Strength 5/5 in all muscle groups tested bilaterally (deltoids, biceps, triceps, wrist extensors, grip, hip flexors, knee extensors, ankle dorsiflexors, plantarflexors). No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses are flexor (downgoing) bilaterally.
